Case study · Video streaming · Mobile · UX research

Making premium worth paying for.

Memento, a free long-form video app, needed to start earning money without adding to subscription fatigue.

I researched what free users would actually pay for and designed Projects, step-by-step courses from Memento creators. Then I tested with 10 participants and rebuilt the screens, the pricing model and even the feature's name around what they showed me.

Role
UX Researcher & Designer (solo)
Timeline
Oct – Nov 2025
Platform
iOS mobile app
Tools
Figma, Google Forms, FigJam

Overview

Memento is a free mobile and web app for long-form, meaningful video. After two years spent building an engaged audience, the startup wanted to add a paid tier. It set two goals: get new users to subscribe, and convert existing free users, both at sign-in and inside the product.

ProblemAd-free viewing isn't enough reason to pay anymore. Viewers already have too many subscriptions, and they cancel the ones they don't use.
SolutionProjects: step-by-step courses from Memento creators, sitting next to Videos and Ripples. Users hear about it during onboarding and unlock it with one clear offer, a 7-day free trial.
Outcome10 moderated sessions (5 new users, 5 returning) surfaced 4 high-severity issues. They led to 6 redesigns, a switch from a paywall to a 7-day trial, and dropping the "Pointer" sub-brand I loved.

The solution

Here's where it ended up: Projects, introduced at the right moments and unlocked with one 7-day trial. Every step is designed around what the user is thinking, and each one moves a metric I can measure. The rest of this case study shows how I got here.

Learns Projects exists during onboarding, then meets it again right after a related video.

Already knows Memento, so there's no onboarding and no pop-up: just a small "New" tip they can choose to open.

Research plan

Business objectives
  1. Get new users to subscribe during sign-up
  2. Convert returning free users, both at sign-in and inside the app
Core research question

What makes someone decide a subscription is worth it, and worth keeping?

I broke it into 8 research questions across 3 themes (mapped below).

1Understand the marketSecondary research + competitive / SWOT analysis of YouTube, Vimeo and Twitch
2Hear from the audienceA survey on what people pay for, keep and cancel
3SynthesizePersona + journey map to find where viewers give up
4Validate the design10 moderated usability sessions in 2 separate groups
Questions × methods

Each question had at least two sources, so no single method decided an answer.

Research questionSecondarySurveyCompetitiveUsabilityWhat I found → where it led
Who & how much
Q1Which demographic buys the most subscriptions?18–24, heavy mobile users, became the target group
Q2What's the most people will comfortably pay?Under ~$11/month for entertainment→ Plans · Fix 04
Q3What bundling makes people more likely to subscribe?Discounts for longer plans + cancel anytime→ Plans · Fix 04
What makes it worth it
Q4How do people decide a subscription is worth it?They keep what they use (4 of 5)→ Key insight
Q6What frustrates viewers on other platforms?Endless searching with no clear path→ Journey map
Q7What are viewers' top requested features?Structure: knowing what to watch next→ Projects concept
Market & creators
Q5Which premium features have worked for competitors?All lead with a free trial; "ad-free" alone isn't enough→ Fix 04
Q8What are creators' top requested features?Direct support converts on Twitch → creator credit→ Open: creator interviews
Participants

18–24 year olds who are very comfortable with tech, spend several hours a day on their phones, and for whom video is a big part of daily life. Mixed gender.

Recruiting

Friends and peers, Springboard participants, and same-day sessions in coffee shops to reach people outside my circle.

Honest limits

The survey had 5 responses, so I treated it as directional and always checked it against secondary data. I didn't let it carry a decision alone.

What the research said

People keep paying for what they use. So premium had to be a tool viewers rely on, not just Memento without ads.

Three findings, each backed by more than one source, shaped every design decision that followed.

01

People cancel what they don't use

  • 30%+cancel within 6 months over cost or low valuePrecedence Research, 2025
  • 22%feel streaming isn't worth the moneyMarketWatch, 2025
  • 4 of 5people I surveyed keep a subscription because they use itMy survey · directional

So I designedA premium tool people use, not just "Memento without ads."

02

People want to try before they pay

  • 3 of 3competitors lead with a free trial (7 days to 1 month)My competitive analysis
  • <$11per month felt comfortable; annual discounts and cancel-anytime terms preferredMy survey
  • Tasteof premium itself converts better than opting into a trial laterKoch & Benlian, 2017

So I designedA 7-day free trial, a discounted 3-month plan and a reminder before billing.

03

Everyone sells "ad-free." Nobody sells structure.

  • 2.8%acquisition rate in 2024, down from 4.1% in 2021, so retention is the priorityRecurly, 2025
  • 0 of 3competitors offer guided, project-based learningMy competitive analysis
  • Loopviewers search, find gaps, then search again until they quitJourney map

So I designedProjects: step-by-step courses that give people a reason to stay.

Confidence
The insight

Every tutorial leaves gaps, so he searches again. More videos don't fix the loop. Order and structure do.

→
So I designed

Projects: lessons in order, resources and a chatroom in one place, so the loop turns into a plan.

The concept

Turn related videos into guided, step-by-step projects, with lessons in order plus resources and a discussion room, so viewers stop guessing what to watch next.

I first called it Pointer; the redesign section explains why it became Projects.

How it makes money

A feature only works if the business works. Crediting creators raised a question I hadn't planned for: who gets paid, and how?

I didn't model the finances in depth, but I mapped how the money could flow so the design stays realistic. This is a direction to validate, not a final model.

1 · Subscribers pay$10.99/mo

or $26 for 3 months. Student and Family tiers. Most start with the 7-day free trial.

→
2 · Memento keeps most of itThe majority

Covers the app, the team and profit. Premium also includes ad-free and offline viewing, not just Projects.

→
3 · A creator poolSplit by watch time

A share goes into one pool, divided by how much of each creator's Projects people actually watch. Unwatched courses earn nothing.

↺ Creators promote their Projects to their own followers, which brings in new subscribers who wouldn't have come otherwise.
Why not make courses in-house?

Producing courses means paying thousands of dollars up front before anyone subscribes. A shared pool grows with revenue, so the catalog can grow without production costs.

Proven model

YouTube Premium and Skillshare both share subscription revenue with creators based on watch time.

The risk I flagged

At launch the pool is small, so early creators might not earn enough to bother. Possible fix: a guaranteed minimum for launch creators and a small, curated first group.

What I'd validate next

Interview creators: is a revenue share worth their time? This also answers research question 8 about creator needs.

Participants understood the pricing. What they didn't understand was what they'd be paying for.

Does a project shown after a free video create intent to pay?Partly. They didn't know what Pointer was.
Is one free lesson enough to show a course's value?No. They asked for a week.

The hard call

The name I loved was the problem.

1 · What I wanted

"Pointer"

Like the dog breed, it points you where to go. I gave it its own name, logo and colors.

"I thought the app was called Memento?"

"Did Memento get renamed to Pointer?"

2 · What testing showed

"A different app"

Confusion in both rounds. Adding "Premium Feature" labels in v1 didn't fix it.

→
3 · What I decided

"Projects"

The cause was a second brand inside an app. A plain word beside Videos and Ripples needs no explaining.

The lesson: users pay for clarity, not my symbolism. Cutting what I loved because the evidence said so was the biggest decision in this project.

Findings → redesign

Each fix shows the wireframe participants tested, my first hi-fi (v1), and the second round (v2). Yellow callouts point to exactly what changed on each screen.

HIGHFIX 01 · "I THOUGHT THE APP WAS CALLED MEMENTO?"
Theme A "What is Pointer?" · fixes 01 02 06↑ All themes

From "Pointer" to Projects

What happened in testing

Participants didn't understand what Pointer was, or that it belonged to Memento. The confusion followed them from the pop-up to the paywall, the welcome screen and the nav tab. It came up in both rounds.

Why this change

The finding was a symptom. The cause was structural: Pointer had its own logo, gradient and wordmark, so tapping into it felt like leaving the app. v1 added "Premium Feature" labels and didn't fix it. v2 removes the sub-brand completely.

The hard callWhy I let go of a name I loved → read the story
Returning users

"Did Memento get renamed to Pointer?"

Returning users already know Memento. In v1 I tried to fix the confusion with a better introduction: a full-screen "Introducing Pointer · Premium Feature" pop-up. Users still read Pointer as its own brand, and a new logo and gradient taking over the screen looked like a rebrand. That's when I renamed it. In v2 there's nothing new to explain, just a small, dismissible "New in Memento" tip on the Projects tab.

HIGHFIX 02
Theme A "What is Pointer?" · fixes 01 02 06↑ All themes

Make a course look like a course

What happened in testing

Course cards used the same gray box and play icon as every video. Participants read the row as recommendations and scrolled right past the core feature.

Why this change

Projects, Videos and Ripples are three kinds of content, so they need three different shapes. In v1, tall portrait cards still read as Ripples (our Shorts). In v2, the shape says "several lessons" before anyone reads the title.

HIGHMEDFIX 03
Theme B Asked too early · fixes 03 04Theme C Value disappeared after paying · fixes 03 05↑ All themes

Sell the whole project, not the next video

What happened in testing

After watching Lesson 1, most participants weren't ready to pay for Lesson 2: "I'd need to see more to know if it's worth it." One video didn't convince them. And nobody noticed Resources or the Chatroom, the perks that make a project more than a playlist.

Why this change

With the 7-day trial, nothing on this page needs a lock. Instead of putting a paywall on every lesson, v2 shows what you get: 5 lessons, Resources and the Chatroom as three clear perks, with one sticky "Start 7-Day Free Trial" button. People decide on the whole project, not on one video.

HIGHMEDFIX 04
Theme B Asked too early · fixes 03 04↑ All themes

From "1 free lesson, then pay" to one 7-day trial

What happened in testing

Participants understood the plans but felt pressured by "48 Hour Offer." One free lesson wasn't enough to judge a course; they asked for a week.

Why this change

The value of structure only shows up over several lessons. My competitive analysis matched what participants said: Twitch, YouTube and Vimeo all lead with a trial. So I dropped the free-lesson model for one clear offer. And because this audience is tired of subscriptions, the reminder before the trial ends answers their biggest fear.

MEDFIX 05
Theme C Value disappeared after paying · fixes 03 05↑ All themes

Confirm the value, then start learning

What happened in testing

The welcome screen was a paragraph of text, and the CTA sent people away from the course they'd chosen.

Why this change

The moment after signing up should confirm "you made the right call" and get users straight back to the project they picked. v1 still had the full-screen Pointer gradient, the look we'd removed everywhere else. v2 is Memento-native and answers this audience's biggest worry, forgetting to cancel, with a simple timeline.

HIGHFIX 06 · NEW IN V2
Theme A "What is Pointer?" · fixes 01 02 06↑ All themes

Introduce Projects in steps, not all at once

What happened in testing

Users either met the feature with no context, or hit a paywall before they understood it.

Why this change

Research said not to sell on day one, but nothing said premium had to stay hidden. Choosing interests is the one moment a new user tells us what they want to learn, so pointing out that those interests have guided projects is useful information, not a pitch.

Bar lengths show the expected shape of the funnel, not real results. Each step's baseline would be set from the first two weeks of live data.

Hypothesis to validate

Do the perks keep people subscribed?

Dotted lines mark the day 5 reminder and day 7 billing. Illustrative curves for the hypothesis I'd test: subscribers who use Resources or Chatroom stay subscribed longer. If it holds, those perks deserve more space before the ask.

Re-test the rename

Do people now see Projects as part of Memento?

In testing, people thought Pointer was a separate app. To check the rename fixed that, I'd show 5 new people the Projects screen for 5 seconds, then ask: "What app is this?"

Goal: at least 4 of 5 answer "Memento." This is a target, not a result.

A/B test

Does the onboarding step pay off?

ASees "Your interests have projects"
vs
BSkips straight to the feed

Measure: % who open a project in week 1. If A doesn't beat B, cut the screen and keep onboarding short.

What I'd do next

Interview creators

Test whether a watch-time revenue share is worth their time. This answers research question 8 on creator needs.

Test Projects as the center tab

The one LOW finding: does a more prominent spot raise discovery without hurting the core video experience?

Add the annual plan

Participants and the survey both asked for a yearly discount next to monthly and 3-month billing.

"Continue learning" on Home

A "Lesson 2 of 5" card at the top of the feed: the strongest everyday reminder of what Premium gives them.

Reusable test kit: the two task scripts, the 4-level severity scale and the findings template are written so any designer or PM can run round 2 without me.

Reflection

Wording and visuals have to be designed together

"Lesson" meant nothing while the card still looked like a video. The UI has to say "course" before the copy does.

When you ask matters as much as how

The same paywall feels like friction or like an invitation depending on whether the user has felt the value first.

Structure beats labels

When users are confused, adding explanation rarely fixes it. Changing what the screen is does.
